summary.one_sentence: Capability Myths Demolished argues that object-capability systems are not just ACLs in another notation: they better support least privilege, delegation, confinement, revocation, and confused-deputy avoidance.
summary.thesis: The paper's core move is to separate muddled capability models and show that object capabilities have different security properties from ACL systems because authority is carried by unforgeable references rather than ambient identity.
summary.why_it_matters: For agents, capabilities are the permission model that sandboxing needs: an agent should not merely be 'running in a box'; it should hold only the specific authority tokens needed for the next action.

prior_state: Access-control-list systems bind authority to subjects, identities, and objects, often relying on ambient authority.
Capability systems were frequently dismissed through three myths: equivalence with ACLs, inability to enforce confinement, and inability to revoke access.
Different papers used different meanings of capability, creating confusion between access-matrix rows, key-like capabilities, and object capabilities.
Least privilege and confused-deputy avoidance were hard to express cleanly in ambient-authority systems.
problem.key_gap: The paper asks whether common objections to capability systems are valid once the object-capability model is distinguished from weaker or misleading capability interpretations.
assumptions: Capabilities are unforgeable and communicable references that combine designation and authority.
Programs can be structured so objects receive references only to the resources they need.
Confinement and revocation are implemented through capability patterns such as membranes, intermediaries, and careful reference distribution.
Security properties should be compared in practical programming models, not only as alternate views of an access matrix.

concepts.name: Object capability
concepts.definition: An unforgeable object reference that both designates an object and authorizes operations on it.

concepts.name: Designation plus authority
concepts.definition: The object-capability principle that the same reference used to name a resource is also the authority to use it.

concepts.name: Ambient authority
concepts.definition: Authority implicitly available because of the caller's identity or environment rather than explicitly passed as a reference.

concepts.name: Confused deputy
concepts.definition: A vulnerability where a program with authority is tricked into misusing that authority on behalf of a less-authorized actor.

concepts.name: Confinement
concepts.definition: Preventing an object or program from communicating or leaking information through undesired channels.

concepts.name: Revocation
concepts.definition: Removing or disabling previously granted access, often through an intermediary object or revocable forwarding reference.

method.core_idea: Compare ACLs-as-columns, capabilities-as-rows, capabilities-as-keys, and object capabilities through concrete security properties, then show that the myths disappear under the object-capability model.
action_grammar: principal/subject: entity attempting to access resources.
object: resource or service being accessed.
ACL entry: object-side rule granting subjects permissions.
capability/reference: unforgeable token held by a subject/object.
delegation: passing a capability to another object.
attenuation: wrapping or narrowing a capability before delegation.
revoker: intermediary object that can later stop forwarding access.
steps: State the equivalence, confinement, and irrevocability myths.
Distinguish four models: ACLs as columns, capabilities as rows, capabilities as keys, and object capabilities.
Define security properties that separate the models rather than collapsing them into an access matrix.
Show why the ACL/capability equivalence comparison misses designation, delegation, and least-privilege behavior.
Analyze confinement in object-capability systems by controlling initial references and communication paths.
Analyze revocation patterns using indirection, membranes, and forwarders.
Connect object capabilities to least privilege and confused-deputy avoidance.

claims.statement: The paper identifies three common capability myths: ACL/capability equivalence, inability to enforce confinement, and inability to revoke capability-based access.
caveats: The paper argues against these myths for object-capability systems, not for every historical system called capability-based.

claims.statement: Confusion comes from treating different capability models as equivalent: rows in an access matrix, keys, and object capabilities have different security properties.
caveats: The terminology is intentionally corrective and may differ from other security texts.

claims.statement: Object-capability systems provide better support for least privilege than ACL systems because authority is passed explicitly as needed rather than drawn from ambient subject identity.
caveats: Least privilege still depends on disciplined program structure and avoiding overbroad capability distribution.

claims.statement: Object capabilities help avoid confused deputy vulnerabilities by binding designation and authority in the same reference.
caveats: Application logic can still misuse authority it legitimately holds.

claims.statement: Capability systems can enforce confinement when the object-capability communication graph and initial references are controlled.
caveats: Covert channels and intentionally supplied communication capabilities remain outside simple confinement claims.

claims.statement: Capability-based access can be revoked through established patterns such as indirection, forwarders, membranes, or revocable references.
caveats: Revocation must be built into the grant path before the capability escapes directly.

claims.statement: The paper's practical recommendation is not to add ambient ACL checks to capabilities, but to use a pure object-capability model with clear reference-passing rules.
caveats: Hybrid systems can still be useful, but they may lose the clean reasoning properties the paper highlights.

evidence.result: The paper explicitly names the Equivalence Myth, Confinement Myth, and Irrevocability Myth as common misconceptions about capability systems.
The authors compare ACLs-as-columns with capabilities-as-rows, capabilities-as-keys, and object capabilities, arguing that many misconceptions arise from switching among these models.
The paper argues that pure capability systems have significant advantages over ACL systems for least-privilege operation because programs can be given only the specific references they need.
The authors connect object capabilities to confused-deputy avoidance by showing that authority follows explicit references rather than ambient identity-based authority.
The paper argues that object-capability systems can enforce confinement by controlling the communication graph and the references initially provided to confined objects.
The paper describes capability revocation through indirection and related object-capability patterns, contradicting the claim that capability access cannot be revoked.
The authors argue that object capabilities, when treated as a coherent model rather than rows in an access matrix, offer useful security properties without bolting on ambient ACL-style checks.

agent_infra_takeaways: An agent permission should be an object it holds, not a row in a global ACL checked against the agent's broad identity.
Tool calls should receive attenuated capabilities: read this file, post to this endpoint, spend up to this amount, for this run id.
Revocation requires indirection. If an agent receives a raw credential, later policy changes may be too late.
Capabilities reduce confused-deputy risk because the tool must be invoked with the specific authority for the specific resource, not ambient user power.
A sandbox without capabilities is incomplete: it limits escape, but it does not model which allowed effects should be possible.
For LLM agents, capability passing also gives an audit trail: every side effect can name the authority object that authorized it.
caveats: The paper is conceptual and model-driven, not an empirical benchmark.
Object-capability reasoning assumes references are unforgeable and communication paths are controlled.
Capabilities do not eliminate all covert channels or all logic bugs.
Revocation must be designed before direct authority leaks; after a raw capability is copied, revocation can be difficult.
Many production systems are hybrids, so importing the paper's conclusions requires identifying which properties the hybrid preserves.
Agent prompt injection can still persuade a model to use capabilities it legitimately holds unless policy checks constrain when they may be exercised.

related_work.title: seL4
related_work.note: seL4 is a concrete verified microkernel whose authorization model is capability-based.

related_work.title: WebAssembly
related_work.note: WASM host imports are naturally capability-shaped authorities supplied by the embedder.

related_work.title: Indirect Prompt Injection
related_work.note: Prompt injection becomes less dangerous when retrieved text cannot exercise capabilities the agent has not been explicitly given.
